--- title: "Multilevel models" subtitle: "Intermediate – respondents in country-years in countries" bibliography: [../references.bib, ../references-new.bib] --- This module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd) works at the level of the individual respondent, where the claim of the EU-frames case was first tested. The case takes its claim from a study by the original author (OA), who reported that poor national economic performance lowers the positive framing of the European Union and fitted that claim to sixteen waves of Eurobarometer respondents with a multilevel model [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic]; the [case study](../cases/eu-frames/index.qmd) tells it in full. The respondents are licensed by GESIS and cannot be shipped, so the module shows the saved output of the models that were fitted once on the licensed file beside the code that produced each output, and its live code runs on a simulated twin of the respondents, whose licence to be used is a validation against the real ones. The module opens with the vocabularies in which different disciplines name the same models, and it meets the module on [panel data](panel-data.qmd), the treatment of the same data at the level of the country-year, at the within–between model of section 5. It is the reading for the second session of day 3 of the [Extended course](../tracks/eu-frames-extended/day-3.qmd) and an optional reading in [stage 4](../tracks/self-study/stage-4.qmd) of the self-study route, and it assumes the first three sections of the panel module, on the linear model and clustered standard errors. ## 1. The vocabularies {#sec-vocabularies} The models of this module go by different names in different disciplines, and a participant who learnt the models in one discipline can fail to recognise them in the vocabulary of another. Sociologists and education researchers speak of multilevel or hierarchical linear models, with pupils nested in schools or respondents in countries as the standard examples [@RaudenbushBryk2002HierarchicalLinearModels; @SnijdersBosker2012MultilevelAnalysisIntroduction], and of contextual effects when an attribute of the group bears on its members. Political scientists meet the same models through time-series cross-section (TSCS) data, a few countries observed over many years [@BeckKatz1995WhatNotTimeseries], and through comparative surveys repeated over time [@Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling; @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel]. Econometricians speak of panel data, of fixed and random effects and of the within and between estimators [@Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross], while psychologists and biostatisticians speak of mixed or mixed-effects models, with random intercepts and random slopes for subjects and items [@PinheiroBates2000MixedEffectsModelsSPLUS; @DeBruineBarr2021UnderstandingMixedeffectsModels]. @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 119] gives three of the names in one breath, multilevel models "(also known as mixed, random effects or hierarchical linear models)", and @tbl-vocabularies sets the terms side by side, row by row, so that a reader trained in any of these traditions can find the terms of their own. | | Sociology and education | Political science | Econometrics | Psychology and biostatistics | |:--|:--|:--|:--|:--| | The model | multilevel model, hierarchical linear model | multilevel model of TSCS data or of comparative longitudinal survey data | random-effects model, unobserved effects model | mixed model, linear mixed-effects model | | The data | respondents (level 1) in countries (level 2), pupils in schools | country-years in countries; respondents in country-years in countries | panel data, units $i$ observed in periods $t$ | repeated measures, longitudinal or clustered data, subjects crossed with items | | An intercept for each group, drawn from a distribution | random intercept, level-2 residual | random intercept | random effect, an unobserved effect assumed to be uncorrelated with the predictors | random intercept, random effect | | An intercept for each group, estimated as a parameter | fixed effects, country dummies | unit fixed effects, country dummies | fixed effects, the within estimator, least squares dummy variables | fixed-effects model for clustered data | | The coefficients shared by all groups | fixed part, fixed effects | coefficients, fixed effects | slope parameters | fixed effects | | A slope that varies across groups | random slope, random coefficient, modelled by a cross-level interaction | random coefficients | random coefficient model | random slope | | The predictor split into the group mean and the departure from it | group-mean centring, within-group and between-group effects, contextual effect | within and between effects, cross-sectional and longitudinal relationships | the between and the within estimator, the Mundlak device, correlated random effects | person-mean or cluster-mean centring, within-person and between-person effects | | The share of the variance between groups | intraclass correlation, variance partition coefficient | intraclass correlation | the share of the unit effect in the variance of the composite error | intraclass correlation | : The same models under the names that four traditions use, row by row. A term can mean one thing in one column and another thing in the next, above all 'fixed effects'. {#tbl-vocabularies} Two terms of the table change their meaning between the columns, and both matter for this case. The first is 'fixed effects'. In econometrics, and in the sociology that follows it [@Allison2009FixedEffectsRegression; @Halaby2004PanelModelsSociological], a fixed effect is an intercept for each group estimated as a parameter, the country dummies of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-fe). In the multilevel and mixed-model traditions, the fixed effects are the coefficients shared by all groups, the fixed part of the model as against its random part. @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 245] note that "[f]ixed effects are usually defined as varying coefficients that are not themselves modeled", while "'fixed-effects models' sometimes refer to regressions in which coefficients do not vary by group (so that they are fixed, not random)". The two senses meet in this case. OA writes of the national indicators that they "are, therefore, included as fixed effects at Level 2 in the models" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 625], in the multilevel sense, since the unemployment rate enters the fixed part of a model with random intercepts for countries and survey waves, and the model has no country dummies at all. The Multi100 analysts KQXUE and C6HJR used fixed effects in the econometric sense, an intercept for each country, so a reader who took the paper and the two reanalyses to share a design because all three mention fixed effects would have misread all three. The second term is 'random effects'. In a multilevel model a random effect is a group intercept or slope drawn from a distribution whose variance the model estimates, while in econometrics the term names, above all, an assumption about such effects, that they are uncorrelated with the predictors, as @Wooldridge2010EconometricAnalysisCross [p. 286] explains and [section 5 of the panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-random-effects) sets out. @HamakerMuthen2020FixedRandomEffects [p. 366] warn psychologists that "the terms fixed effect and random effect, tend to be used differently in these disciplines than how they are typically used in the psychological literature", and their article shows that the concern of econometricians about fixed against random effects and the concern of the multilevel literature about how to centre a predictor "are actually addressing the same underlying issue" (p. 365), the issue that section 5 takes up. This module follows where it can the advice of @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 246], which is to "avoid the terms 'fixed' and 'random' entirely, and focus on the description of the model itself (for example, varying intercepts and constant slopes)". It keeps 'fixed effects' for the econometric sense and writes 'the coefficients of the fixed part' for the multilevel one. In R the distinction is written into the syntax. `fixest::feols(y ~ x | cntry)` gives each country an intercept of its own, estimated as a parameter, while `lme4::lmer(y ~ x + (1 | cntry))` draws the country intercepts from a distribution and estimates its variance. Inside `lmer()`, `(1 + x | cntry)` lets the slope of `x` vary by country as well, `(1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year)` nests country-years in countries, and `(1 | cntry) + (1 | year)` crosses countries with years. ## 2. The level of analysis {#sec-why} A claim about the effect of a context can be read at two levels. In the EU-frames case the claim is about countries, and it asks whether the people of a country frame the EU less positively when their national economy performs badly. The same words license a second reading. Perhaps unemployed *people* frame the EU differently, so that a country with more of them shows a lower average without anything having changed for anyone else. The first reading is **contextual**, in that living through high unemployment changes how everyone frames the EU, and the second is **compositional**, in that the mix of people changes while each person frames the EU as before, and a country-year panel cannot separate the two readings, because it contains no people. Reading an association among aggregates as if it held among individuals is the problem of ecological inference set out by @Robinson1950EcologicalCorrelationsBehavior, and @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 122] warns that an analysis of aggregated survey data "risks committing an ecological fallacy in which aggregate-level relationships are erroneously assumed also to hold for the individual units on which the pre-aggregated data were collected". The multilevel model is the standard way of keeping both levels in one analysis: the respondents enter it as individuals, and the country-years and countries as the contexts in which the respondents answered. Section 7 uses it to ask how much of the national association the composition of the respondents could account for. ## 3. Respondents and the simulated twin {#sec-twin} The Eurobarometer microdata behind the published result are licensed by GESIS and cannot be redistributed. They can still be obtained: the sixteen survey files can be downloaded with a free GESIS account, and the build script in the workspace turns them into one respondent file, `data_private/eb_respondents.rds`, whose [codebook](../cases/eu-frames/data/eb_respondents_codebook.md) is published even though the file is not. The [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) explains the download, and the [data management module](data-management.qmd) the build. Every number on this page labelled 'real' was computed on that file by a script of the repository for the site, named in the [sources](#sec-sources) at the end of the page, and a reader who holds the file can rerun the script. What the course ships is a **synthetic twin**: `EUframes_person_full.csv`, 41,660 simulated respondents across the real 270 country-years, with every variable that the published regressions of OA use. No real respondent appears in it. [The simulation module](simulation.qmd#sec-dgp) explains how it is built. In short, the characteristics of a simulated respondent come from a correlation structure estimated on the real file, and the answers from a model of the survey instrument conditional on those characteristics. The live code of this page runs on the twin, so that the page renders for everyone, and swapping the twin for the respondent file is a one-line change. A number from the twin is licensed by its validation against the real respondents: the same model was fitted to the real respondents and to the twin, and the two sets of coefficients were compared. ::: {#tbl-validation .cell tbl-cap='Every coefficient of the published model of OA without its cross-level interactions, fitted on the 407,144 real respondents with complete covariates and on the twin. The last column is the largest difference over the two-sample standard error. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/twin_validation.csv`.'} ```{.r .cell-code} valid |> dplyr::summarise( `coefficients compared` = dplyr::n(), `within 1 standard error` = sum(abs(z) < 1), `within 2 standard errors` = sum(abs(z) < 2), `largest discrepancy` = round(max(abs(z)), 2)) |> tinytable::tt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
coefficients compared within 1 standard error within 2 standard errors largest discrepancy
64 46 60 2.87
``` ::: ::: 60 of 64 agree within two standard errors, where roughly three would be expected to fall outside by chance alone, and the comparison stored in `_model-outputs/twin_validation.csv` can be read line by line. Two cautions apply to that result. The yardstick above is the **two-sample** standard error, which asks whether a difference exceeds the sampling noise of the twin itself, the question that a reader quoting one of its numbers has. Judged instead against the precision that 407,144 respondents afford, only 39 agree, because the twin holds a tenth as many people and cannot stand in at full precision. And the model validated is the specification of OA with its cross-level interactions removed. The twin reproduces that model, but it is not validated for the interacted form and should not be quoted for it. ### The limits of the twin {#sec-limits} **The twin will support** the specification validated above and models close to it: the four framing dimensions, the published covariate set, random structures for countries and country-years, and the arithmetic of composition against context. Coefficients from those models may be quoted with the validation table beside them. **It will not support** three things. It cannot support anything at the level of the survey **wave**, because the twin is built on 270 country-years and its finest cluster is the country-year, while the real file has sixteen waves across ten years. It cannot support the **interacted** form of the published model, which was excluded from the validation because a synthesis built to reproduce a covariance structure does not reproduce a cross-level interaction unless one is put into it. And it cannot support analyses of **individual framing items**, since the twin reproduces the average salience of each item but not its variation from country to country, a limit that does not affect any model using the four dimension scores, which covers every model on this page. The [codebook of the twin](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_person_full_codebook.md) adds a fourth limit: slopes of unemployment fitted to the cell means of the twin are about a sixth larger in magnitude than those of the panel, a known property of the generator that the course leaves in place. **Its weight is not a survey weight.** The variable `w1` reverses an over-sampling of younger respondents that the generator introduces so that weighting has something to correct. It is a teaching device with a known answer and should not be read as the design weight of the Eurobarometer. ## 4. The multilevel model {#sec-multilevel} Every model of the panel module was fitted at the level of the country-year, whereas OA worked with individual respondents, and so does this section, on 416,698 respondents rebuilt from the sixteen GESIS waves. A **multilevel model** fits the respondents directly while representing the nesting explicitly: respondents within country-years, and country-years within countries. Written at its three levels, with $i$ indexing respondents, the model reads $$ y_{i(ct)} = \pi_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict} \qquad\qquad \text{(respondents around the mean of their cell)} $$ $$ \pi_{ct} = \alpha_c + \beta x_{ct} + r_{ct} \qquad \text{(cell means moved by unemployment)} $$ $$ \alpha_c = \gamma_0 + v_c \qquad\qquad\quad \text{(countries around the grand mean)} $$ or, substituted into one line, $$ y_{ict} = \gamma_0 + \beta x_{ct} + v_c + r_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict} $$ with $v_c \sim N(0, \sigma_v^2)$, $r_{ct} \sim N(0, \sigma_r^2)$ and $\varepsilon_{ict} \sim N(0, \sigma_\varepsilon^2)$. Three variance components now share the noise: $\sigma_v^2$ for durable differences between countries, $\sigma_r^2$ for the departures of country-years from their country, and $\sigma_\varepsilon^2$ for differences between people inside a cell. The fixed part, $\gamma_0 + \beta x_{ct}$, is shared by everyone, and the random part is a sum of draws at each level. This is the random-effects model of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-random-effects) generalised, and `(1 | group)` in the notation of `lmer()` declares each random intercept. OA describes the same structure with the survey wave as the middle level: "citizens (Level 1; N: 390,373) are sampled within 16 EB waves (Level 2) that repeatedly took place within the 27 EU countries (Level 3)" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 623]. @fig-ml-structure draws the structure on a small simulated example. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(11) countries <- c("Country A", "Country B", "Country C") country_eff <- c(-0.08, 0.02, 0.09) toy_cells <- tidyr::expand_grid(country = countries, year = c("2008", "2009")) |> dplyr::mutate(cell_mu = 0.5 + rep(country_eff, each = 2) + rnorm(6, 0, 0.045)) # r-style: keep – data_modify() draws the random numbers twice and so changes the figure toy <- toy_cells |> dplyr::slice(rep(1:6, each = 14)) |> dplyr::mutate(y = cell_mu + rnorm(84, 0, 0.09)) # r-style: keep – as above country_means <- toy_cells |> datawizard::data_summary(mu = mean(cell_mu), by = "country") ggplot2::ggplot(toy, ggplot2::aes(year, y)) + ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = mean(toy_cells$cell_mu), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") + ggplot2::geom_hline(data = country_means, ggplot2::aes(yintercept = mu), colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.7) + ggplot2::geom_jitter(width = 0.12, height = 0, colour = "grey65", size = 1.4) + ggplot2::stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "crossbar", width = 0.4, colour = "#a10000", linewidth = 0.5) + ggplot2::facet_grid(cols = ggplot2::vars(country)) + ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "framing score") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The three levels of the multilevel model, illustrated with simulated data: three countries, two survey years each, fourteen respondents in each cell. Respondents (grey points) scatter around the mean of their country-year cell (red bars), the variation between persons. Cell means scatter around the level of their own country (solid blue line), which is the country-year component. And the levels of the countries scatter around the grand mean (dashed line), the country component. A multilevel model estimates one variance for each of those three kinds of scatter.](multilevel_files/figure-html/fig-ml-structure-1.png){#fig-ml-structure width=768} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## How the outputs of this section were produced The respondent file cannot ship with the course, so the models of this section that are fitted to it are displayed rather than executed on the page. The outputs of the three models below were produced by the script `companion/_model-outputs/fit_models.R`, and the numbers behind those outputs by `fit_person_multilevel.R` in the same folder, both run on the machine of the facilitator against the rebuilt respondent file; the text shown is verbatim R output, and the code above each output is the code that produced it. These are single, simple fits, chosen to teach how the output of each method is read. To run them yourself you need the raw waves under your own free GESIS registration, which the [data sources module](data-sources.qmd#sec-gesis) walks through, while the same three models run on the twin when this page is built. ::: ### Levels and evidence {#sec-levels} The first fit declares only the country level, which is too few levels for these data: ```r person <- readRDS("data_private/eb_respondents.rds") # 416,698 respondents, built by prep/01_build_respondents.R m_two <- lmerTest::lmer(cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), data = person) summary(m_two) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method ['lmerModLmerTest'] Formula: cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) Data: person REML criterion at convergence: 353436.4 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.65509 -0.93396 0.00253 1.03162 1.80580 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. cntry (Intercept) 0.003941 0.06278 Residual 0.136677 0.36970 Number of obs: 416698, groups: cntry, 27 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5.474e-01 1.222e-02 2.705e+01 44.80 <2e-16 *** unemp -4.790e-03 1.953e-04 3.912e+05 -24.52 <2e-16 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) unemp -0.140 ``` ::: ::: Read the output in two blocks. The `Random effects` block reports the estimated variance components, $\hat\sigma_v^2 = 0.0039$ for countries and $\hat\sigma_\varepsilon^2 = 0.1367$ for respondents, and the `Fixed effects` table, which holds the coefficients of the fixed part, reads like an `lm()` coefficient table with one addition, a `df` column computed by the approximation of Satterthwaite in lmerTest [@KuznetsovaEtAl2017LmerTestPackageTests], which estimates how many independent pieces of information support each `t`. That column shows the flaw in this model. A slope of −0.0048 with t = −24.5 on **391,197 degrees of freedom** looks like overwhelming evidence, but the model has been allowed to treat every respondent as fresh information about unemployment, when every respondent in a country-year shares one unemployment value. The predictor has only 270 distinct values, so a model whose degrees of freedom run to six figures is counting people as if they were countries. @Schmidt-CatranFairbrother2016RandomEffectsMultilevel [p. 25] describe the consequence for such two-level designs: variables of the country-year "are implicitly taken as individual-level variables, inflating the degrees of freedom and deflating the SEs", since "[a] cluster-level variable is defined by the fact that it is constant within clusters". Declaring the country-year level as well changes the result: ```r m_three <- lmerTest::lmer(cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year), data = person) summary(m_three) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method ['lmerModLmerTest'] Formula: cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year) Data: person REML criterion at convergence: 350414.6 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.77238 -0.96186 0.01493 0.99635 1.89818 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. cntry:year (Intercept) 0.001485 0.03853 cntry (Intercept) 0.003759 0.06131 Residual 0.135469 0.36806 Number of obs: 416698, groups: cntry:year, 270; cntry, 27 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 5.526e-01 1.393e-02 4.441e+01 39.682 < 2e-16 *** unemp -5.237e-03 8.021e-04 2.531e+02 -6.528 3.61e-10 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) unemp -0.502 ``` ::: ::: The slope barely moves (−0.0052), while its standard error grows 4.1-fold, the `t` falls from −24.5 to −6.5, and the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom collapse to **253**. That is the scale of the 270 cells, not of the 416,698 respondents, because the predictor varies only between cells. The new variance component ($\hat\sigma_r^2 = 0.0015$) is small in absolute terms, yet acknowledging it changes the inference several-fold. The random-intercept model of the aggregate panel, fitted beside it, gives a slope of −0.0053 with t = −6.6. Once the error structure matches the real structure of the data, modelling 416,698 people and modelling their 270 cell means give much the same answer about a predictor at the level of the country-year, which is why the course can teach the case from the shipped panel. ### Random slopes {#sec-slopes} The multilevel framework adds something new once more than the intercept is allowed to vary. A **random slope** lets each country have its own unemployment coefficient, drawn from a distribution whose spread is estimated, $$ y_{ict} = \gamma_0 + (\beta + b_c)\, x_{ct} + v_c + r_{ct} + \varepsilon_{ict}, \qquad b_c \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2) $$ and the third fit on the respondents adds one: ```r m_slopes <- lmerTest::lmer(cosmo ~ unemp + (1 + unemp | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year), data = person) summary(m_slopes) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method ['lmerModLmerTest'] Formula: cosmo ~ unemp + (1 + unemp | cntry) + (1 | cntry:year) Data: person REML criterion at convergence: 350388.3 Scaled residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -1.76748 -0.95971 0.01417 0.99887 1.89847 Random effects: Groups Name Variance Std.Dev. Corr cntry:year (Intercept) 1.201e-03 0.034660 cntry (Intercept) 4.133e-03 0.064291 unemp 3.713e-05 0.006093 -0.44 Residual 1.355e-01 0.368061 Number of obs: 416698, groups: cntry:year, 270; cntry, 27 Fixed effects: Estimate Std. Error df t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 0.553728 0.015552 20.196050 35.606 < 2e-16 *** unemp -0.005712 0.001684 18.815257 -3.392 0.00309 ** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Correlation of Fixed Effects: (Intr) unemp -0.658 ``` ::: ::: In the `Random effects` block, the standard deviation of the slope is 0.0061, larger in magnitude than the mean slope of −0.0057 itself, so the countries do not share one unemployment slope. The model estimates that the slope ranges from clearly negative in some countries to positive in others, with the average lying where the earlier fits put it, and the `Corr` of −0.44 adds that countries with higher intercepts tend to have more negative slopes. The degrees of freedom of the slope in the fixed part are now about **19**, because once each country contributes mainly to its own slope, the effective evidence for the *average* slope is the 27 countries, not the 270 cells, and the `df` column in this way tracks where the information comes from. Two of the five Multi100 analysts worked at this level, and their results, as Multi100 converted them to partial correlations, mark the two ends of the range recorded for the five. The analyst KEVF1 (in R) reported t = −5.90 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of about 136, converting to a partial correlation of −0.452. The analyst PRL47 (in Stata) reported z = −3.59 with the count of 394,575 respondents standing in for the degrees of freedom, converting to −0.006. The two used the same data and the same family of models and found the same negative direction, yet their converted effect sizes differ 79-fold, almost entirely because of the convention for the degrees of freedom. Across the three model declarations above, the degrees of freedom moved from 391,197 to 253 to 19. The unit of analysis, and the error structure declared around it, is therefore a choice of **estimand**, a decision about what 'the effect' refers to and which draws of the world would count as replications. The aggregated models answer a question about country-years. The models of the respondents appear to answer one about people, but with a predictor that varies only by country-year those models mostly ask the same question again with more elaborate accounting for the errors. The course places each of the five results on the degrees of freedom of its own inference, and the [case page](../cases/eu-frames/index.qmd#sec-recorded) sets that placement beside the values that Multi100 recorded, while the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-onescale) shows how much the converted effect sizes depend on the degrees of freedom. The three structures run on the twin when this page is built, and @tbl-levels sets the fits on the twin beside the values from the 416,698 real respondents. ::: {#tbl-levels .cell tbl-cap='The unemployment coefficient on the cosmopolitan scale under three random structures, fitted on the twin when the page is built, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The real values are read from `companion/_model-outputs/person_multilevel_real.csv`, written by the same models on the licensed respondents.'} ```{.r .cell-code} structures <- list( "countries" = cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry), "countries and country-years" = cosmo ~ unemp + (1 | cntry) + (1 | cy), "the same, with a random slope" = cosmo ~ unemp + (1 + unemp | cntry) + (1 | cy)) keys <- c("two_level", "three_level", "slopes") # dplyr inside the lambda, because datawizard does not find the arguments of a lambda purrr::imap(structures, \(f, nm) { m <- lmerTest::lmer(f, data = twin) p <- coef(summary(m))["unemp", ] real_row <- real_unemp |> dplyr::filter(model == keys[match(nm, names(structures))]) tibble::tibble(`random intercepts for` = nm, `twin: slope` = p[["Estimate"]], `twin: t` = p[["t value"]], `twin: df` = p[["df"]], `real: slope` = real_row$value, `real: df` = real_row$df) }) |> purrr::list_rbind() |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c(`twin: slope`, `real: slope`), \(x) insight::format_value(x, digits = 5, style_negative = "minus")), `twin: t` = insight::format_value(`twin: t`, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus"), dplyr::across(c(`twin: df`, `real: df`), \(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ","))) |> tinytable::tt() |> tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:6, align = "r") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}

The share of the variance that lies between the groups is what multilevel modellers call the intraclass correlation, and here it is 4.6% for countries and country-years together. The small share reflects the shape of the outcome at this level. A respondent who mentions two things and finds one of them cosmopolitan scores exactly one half, so the score is bounded, takes only a few values, and its scatter within any cell is enormous compared with the differences between cells. That is also why so many respondents add so little precision to the estimate for a predictor at the level of the country-year. The component for country-years on the twin is about 16% larger than the real one, because the cells of the twin hold a tenth as many respondents, so their means are noisier, and some of that sampling noise is attributed to the cell level rather than to people, while the components for countries and for persons agree with the real ones to within a few per cent. Whenever the predictor is measured at a higher level, a sample size counted in persons suggests a precision that the design does not have. The number of higher-level units sets the limit, and 27 countries are few. Simulating multilevel models of country data, @BryanJenkins2016MultilevelModellingCountry [p. 3] conclude that "[w]ith large sample sizes of individuals within each country but only a small number of countries, analysts can reliably estimate individual-level effects but estimates of parameters summarizing country effects are likely to be unreliable", and @Stegmueller2013HowManyCountries [p. 748] finds that with few countries "maximum likelihood estimates and confidence intervals can be severely biased, especially in models including cross-level interactions". The [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) makes the same point for the country-year panel, where CR2 errors with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom count how many of the 27 countries effectively carry the information. ## 5. The within–between model {#sec-rewb} The [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-within-between) fits the within–between model on the 270 country-years and reads it as an econometrician would, as the device of @Mundlak1978PoolingTimeSeries that reproduces the fixed-effects slope inside a random-effects model; the code and the numbers of the fit are there. Read from the multilevel side, the same fit is a two-level model in which the country-years are the units at level 1 and the countries the units at level 2, the arrangement in which, as @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 121] notes, TSCS data "can be analyzed using multilevel models in which country-observations are the level-1 units, countries are the level-2 units and level-2 random intercepts are estimated from the data". The unemployment rate of a country-year is then a level-1 predictor, and the within–between model enters it centred on the mean of its country, together with that mean as a predictor at level 2. Centring within clusters, as the multilevel literature calls the step, is in the words of @HamakerMuthen2020FixedRandomEffects [p. 371] "arguably the gold standard in the multilevel literature at this point", because it yields the slope within the clusters however the clusters differ. The coefficient on the uncentred predictor of a random-intercept model is, by contrast, what @RaudenbushBryk2002HierarchicalLinearModels [p. 139] call "an uninterpretable blend" of the two slopes when they differ, and the random-intercept slope of the panel turned out to be such a blend. The difference between the two slopes has a reading of its own in the multilevel tradition. Raudenbush and Bryk say that contextual effects, "of enduring interest in organizational sociology", occur "when the aggregate of a person-level characteristic ... is related to the outcome ... even after controlling for the effect of the individual characteristic" (p. 139), and they measure the effect as the between slope minus the within slope, $\beta_c = \beta_b - \beta_w$, "the expected difference in the outcomes between two students who have the same individual SES, but who attend schools differing by one unit in mean SES" (p. 141). On the panel that difference is the coefficient on the country mean in the Mundlak form, positive and different from zero under every test that the panel module applies. Read in the terms of Raudenbush and Bryk, it is the expected difference in cosmopolitan framing between two country-years with the same unemployment rate in countries whose average rates over the decade differ by one point, a comparison across countries that a claim about change within them does not ask for. @BellEtAl2019FixedRandomEffects [p. 1057] read the Hausman test of the panel module in the same terms, as a test of whether there is a contextual effect. With respondents in the model the decomposition takes one step more. @Fairbrother2013TwoMultilevelModeling [p. 124] observes that the usual model for comparative surveys repeated over time, with respondents in country-years in countries and a single coefficient on a variable of the country-year, "effectively assumes that the cross-sectional and longitudinal relationships between x and y are the same", and he proposes to split such a variable into the mean of each country and the departure of each country-year from it, both entered beside the characteristics of the respondents, together with a term for time. The published model of OA, to which the next section turns, has the single coefficient of the first form, and section 8 shows what a term for the years does to it. ## 6. Individual effects and aggregate associations {#sec-composition} The two coefficients of the previous section apply to different units, so they are not rival explanations of one thing. The individual effect applies to whoever is unemployed, and the contextual effect applies to everyone, in the sense of section 5: the coefficient on the national rate, in a model that holds the employment status of the respondent constant, is what Raudenbush and Bryk call a contextual effect. The question is how much of the association at the level of the country the individual effect could account for. That depends on a quantity which neither coefficient contains, namely how much the unemployment rate of a country changes *who is in the sample*. Measured on the real respondents, a one-point rise in the published rate adds 0.0074 to the share of respondents who are themselves unemployed, well under one percentage point. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} b_ind <- lme4::fixef(m_cosmo)[["sesunemployed"]] b_ctx <- lme4::fixef(m_cosmo)[["munemp"]] grad_w <- grad$gradient[2] tibble::tibble( quantity = c("individual effect of being unemployed", "extra unemployed share per point of the national rate", "compositional contribution to the country-level slope", "the country-level slope itself", "compositional share of it"), value = c(b_ind, grad_w, b_ind * grad_w, b_ctx, b_ind * grad_w / b_ctx)) |> datawizard::data_modify(value = signif(value, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 2 quantity value 1 individual effect of being unemployed -0.0278 2 extra unemployed share per point of the national rate 0.00743 3 compositional contribution to the country-level slope -0.000207 4 the country-level slope itself -0.00544 5 compositional share of it 0.038 ``` ::: ::: So the compositional path accounts for roughly 3.8% of the association at the level of the country, because an effect several times the size, spread over a group that barely grows, moves the average hardly at all. That figure is computed from the coefficients of the twin itself, and the contrast for the unemployed is where the twin performs worst: it comes back at −0.0278 against −0.0350 on the real respondents, the largest single discrepancy in the validation table. Using the real values the compositional share is 4.5% rather than 3.8%. Both are small, so the conclusion does not depend on which is used, even though the twin is visibly imperfect on this coefficient. This calculation should be asked for whenever an aggregate association is explained by 'it must be the people who changed'. It is rarely done, and when it is done the compositional explanation usually does not hold up. It needs an individual-level effect *and* a prevalence gradient, meaning the amount by which the share of people in the group rises as the aggregate predictor rises, and the second is usually assumed, although it can be measured. The [simulation module](simulation.qmd#sec-composition) builds data in which the answer is known in advance. ## 8. Two designs {#sec-designs} The course panel and the model of OA are both defensible readings of the same claim, and they do not agree. Fitted with growth beside unemployment, as the paper fits it, the two-way design of the panel gives a smaller unemployment slope than the published design, and the reason lies in the years. Bounded outcomes {#sec-glm} One assumption has gone unexamined in every model so far: that a Gaussian linear model is the right shape for this outcome. Strictly, it never was. Every framing scale in this case is bounded between 0 and 1, whereas a Gaussian model has unbounded support, so a straight line extended far enough always predicts impossible values, and nothing inside `lm()` or `lmer()` takes the bounds into account. The assumption is wrong at both levels of the data. What differs between the levels is how much that matters, as the two panels of @fig-outcome-scales show. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} p_person <- ggplot2::ggplot(cosmo_dist, ggplot2::aes(cosmo, n_respondents / sum(n_respondents))) + ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.022, fill = "#0e3b6a") + ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-0.02, 1.02)) + ggplot2::labs(title = paste(format(sum(cosmo_dist$n_respondents), big.mark = ","), "respondents"), x = "cosmopolitan framing score", y = "share of respondents") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) p_cells <- ggplot2::ggplot(panel, ggplot2::aes(mcosmo)) + ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.025, boundary = 0, fill = "#0e3b6a") + ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) + ggplot2::labs(title = "270 country-year means", x = "mean cosmopolitan framing", y = "count of cells") + ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) patchwork::wrap_plots(p_person, p_cells) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same outcome at two levels. Fitted values from the models of the panel module never approach the bounds, the probability that the Gaussian error places beyond them is negligible, and the approximation is safe *in practice*, because of where this particular outcome happens to lie and not because the model allows for the bounds. That is a judgement to make consciously, and to make again whenever an outcome drifts towards its floor or ceiling. At the level of the respondent (left panel) the judgement goes the other way. The score of a respondent is the share of the mentioned items that are cosmopolitan, 26% of all respondents sit at exactly 0 and another 25% at exactly 1, and a Gaussian model treats those masses as ordinary noise around a middle that describes almost nobody. The family of **generalised linear models** (GLMs) fixes the shape problem by modelling a *transformed* mean, $$ g\!\left( \mathbb{E}[y_i] \right) = \eta_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i $$ in which the **linear predictor** $\eta_i$ stays a familiar straight line, the **link function** $g$ maps the constrained mean of the outcome onto the unconstrained line, and a distribution suited to the values that the outcome can take replaces the Gaussian. The classic member is **logistic regression**, for binary outcomes, with the log-odds link, here for the outcome collapsed to 'mentions at least one cosmopolitan item': $$ \log \frac{p_i}{1 - p_i} = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i, \qquad p_i = \Pr(y_i = 1) $$ ```r m_logit <- glm(I(cosmo > 0) ~ unemp, family = binomial(), data = person) summary(m_logit) ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: glm(formula = I(cosmo > 0) ~ unemp, family = binomial(), data = person) Coefficients: Estimate Std. The slope of −0.027 is a change in *log-odds* for each point of unemployment, exponentiating gives an odds ratio of $e^{−0.027} \approx 0.974$, and the 'divide by 4 rule' of @GelmanHill2007DataAnalysisUsing [p. 82] bounds the change in probability at about −0.7 percentage points for each point of unemployment. The generalised and the multilevel extensions deal with separate problems, and this outcome needs both at once. For a *bounded continuous* outcome the classical tool is **beta regression**, which models a variable on the open interval (0, 1) with a mean linked by the logit and a precision parameter $\phi$. For this variable its defect is the masses at the endpoints, because the beta distribution places no probability at exactly 0 or 1, and the traditional workaround, nudging the data inward, is the kind of silent choice that this course sets out to make visible. **Ordered beta regression** [@Kubinec2023OrderedBetaRegression] builds the endpoints into the model. A single model uses ordered cutpoints to decide whether an observation is exactly 0, in between, or exactly 1, with a beta distribution for the middle, and one vector of coefficients governs all three parts, so that the slope keeps a single interpretation. On the country-year panel the beta family is a check of functional form rather than a repair. The cell means lie strictly inside the unit interval, as the right panel above showed, with none of the masses at the endpoints that force the ordered beta model on the respondents, so a plain beta regression with the logit link is well defined there, with the fixed effects entered as country and year dummies. It respects the bounds of a share and lets the variance shrink near them, which matters most for the utilitarian scale, whose cell means come down to 0.03. The beta model describes the same conditional mean as the linear one through a link, so its slope is on the logit scale, and its z statistic is converted to a partial correlation on the residual degrees of freedom of the fit, as the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-onescale) describes. At the reproduced specification the slope on the logit scale is −0.0140, with a claim-aligned partial correlation of −0.258 against −0.242 for the linear fit. Swapped into every specification of the curve, the beta family puts 98.1% of the fits below zero, as many as the linear family does, and moves the partial correlation by a median of −0.018. The family stays off the curve for a reason of inference rather than of fit. The beta fits share the serial correlation of the linear ones and need a cluster-robust test as much, but the clubSandwich package, which computes the CR2 test of the [panel module](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference), does not cover beta regression, so the beta fits can only be tested by errors clustered by country on G − 1 degrees of freedom, the rule that overstates the evidence when a few countries carry most of the variation. Under that rule 80.7% of the beta twins lie below zero with p < 0.05, against 80.1% of the linear specifications under the same rule, so the two families agree, and keeping both would double the number of points on the curve without adding an answer while putting two rules of significance on one chart. The [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd#level-estimation) records the option among the decisions about the model. At the level of the respondent the beta likelihood is unavailable, because the scales of the respondents place real mass on exact zeros and ones, and the ordered beta model above, or a fractional-response binomial model with the logit link, takes its place. The general point holds at both levels. A family of models is one more fork, and because a universe of specifications grows geometrically one defensible fork at a time, the discipline is to state in advance which forks you consider defensible and why, which is the job of a preregistration, rather than to run the largest universe that you can afford. ## 11. The education gap {#sec-claim2} The second hypothesis of the paper is about people inside countries, and it cannot be tested on the 270-row panel at all. The abstract states the finding in one sentence, which serves as the claim card for a second replication exercise in the style of the first: > "…high unemployment rates affect the EU framing of high-educated citizens to a larger extent…" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 619], or, in other words from the same abstract, "high unemployment rates are associated with a smaller gap between high- and low-educated citizens in the way they frame the EU". > **Unemployment × high education → cosmopolitan EU framing: b = −0.0031, t = −6.93, p < .001** (Table 3, Model 1), beside an education gap of b = 0.0771 (t = 41.79) and an unemployment slope of b = −0.0034 (t = −4.03) at the lowest education band. The estimand statement, in the form that the [specification menu](../cases/eu-frames/menu.qmd#the-estimand-statement) uses, reads: among respondents in the 27 member states surveyed between 2004 and 2013, the difference between high- and low-educated respondents in the association between the national unemployment rate, measured as the World Bank series, and cosmopolitan EU framing, built as the share of the mentions of a respondent, comparing each country with itself over time. The quantity is an interaction, the amount by which the association with unemployment differs between education bands, and that is what makes the claim one about individuals. Education is a property of respondents and unemployment a property of country-years, and the question is whether people who differ on the first respond differently to the second. Multilevel modellers call such a term a **cross-level interaction**, which @HeisigSchaeffer2019WhyYouShould [p. 258] describe as "a specific type of context effect that may be understood as an upper-level variable moderating the association between a lower-level predictor and the outcome". **Three ways to estimate it.** The published model is a three-level random-intercept model with the interaction terms and the full set of covariates, fitted on the respondents. The same interaction can be fitted with country and year fixed effects instead of random intercepts. Those effects remove the average level of framing in each country and the shocks common to all countries in a year. They do not absorb the national unemployment rate, which moves within each country from one year to the next, so both its slope and the difference of that slope between bands remain estimable. Because the three bands of a country share one country effect, the difference between bands draws on differences between countries in the size of the education gap as well as on movement within each country. And the interaction can be fitted on cells rather than respondents. The [panel by education band](../cases/eu-frames/data/EUframes_cy_edu_codebook.md) holds one row for each country, year and band, and a fixed-effects regression on its 810 rows, weighted by the respondents behind each mean, addresses the same question with the same data at the aggregate level. The fixed-effects rows change the design instead. The fixed-effects design estimates a slope for unemployment as well as its difference between bands, because the national rate moves within each country from year to year and the country and year effects do not absorb it. Under the published rule the slope is −0.0030 (t = −3.45), against −0.0044 (t = −5.74) in the published design. The interaction under the published rule falls further with fixed effects, from −0.0029 to −0.0014 (t = −1.75), and under the zero rule it is practically zero, −0.00007. The cell row, fitted on 810 aggregates that anyone can download, agrees with the fixed-effects row of the respondents under the same rule on the unemployment slope and on both interactions, which confirms that for the interaction the aggregate route addresses the same question as the route through the respondents. The two rows differ on the education gap, 0.1637 in the cells against 0.1174 among the respondents, and the difference comes mainly from the covariates, since the model of the respondents holds sex, age, occupation and size of community constant, while the cell model holds none of them. Taken as a whole, the table shows the claim holding under the design and the rule that OA used, and weakening step by step as the fixed-effects design replaces the published one and as the respondents who named nothing are kept rather than dropped. The unemployment slope repeats the finding of [section 8](#sec-designs), since the design of OA includes no year effects and unemployment and framing moved everywhere at once in 2009. The interaction does not follow that reasoning, because year effects shared by the three bands cannot remove a shock in which the bands moved differently. The fixed-effects rows also drop the random intercepts for country-waves, and on the 810 cells that is the change which moves the interaction: a random-intercept model with intercepts for countries and country-years gives −0.00102 without year effects and −0.00098 with them, and +0.00021 once the intercepts for country-years are removed. A footnote of the paper reports that "[r]andom slopes models show similar regression coefficients to the random intercept model" [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic, p. 631, n. 3], but similar coefficients say nothing about the standard errors on which the verdict depends, so a random slope for education across countries is one of the decisions that a reanalysis of this claim has to make. **A replication exercise of your own.** The pieces for a second exercise in the style of the first are all on this page: a claim card, an estimand statement, a public dataset on which the aggregate design runs in the browser lab or the workspace, the respondent file for anyone who built it, and the published values of OA to reproduce.
